opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and my answer has definitely shifted over the years.

Early in my career, especially during my PhD, I thought valuable research meant novelty in a fairly narrow sense: a clever new idea, a new formulation, a few points of improvement on a benchmark, and a paper accepted at a top conference. That was the scoreboard everyone around me was using, so I used it too. Those things aren't meaningless; they train you to think rigorously and to execute.

Over time, though, especially after joining industry and working on generative models, I started asking a different question: if this work disappeared tomorrow, would anyone notice? Would anyone's work actually change? That's a much harsher test. Many papers, including some of my own, wouldn't pass it.

Now I think about value in a few ways.

First, does it open a door? The most valuable work isn't always the most polished. It's the work that makes a new kind of problem tractable, so other people can build on it. When GANs started producing realistic images, the specific architectures mattered less than the realization that you could actually synthesize content, and then a whole community ran with it.

Second, does it compound? I've come to appreciate infrastructure, data, and models that others can use. A strong open model or a well-built pipeline can enable hundreds of projects you never imagined. Early on I might have seen that as engineering rather than research. Now I think it's often where the real leverage is.

Third, is it pointed at a problem that matters in the long run? For me lately that's been world models and physical AI: systems that understand how the world evolves, so robots and autonomous machines can learn and be tested in simulation before acting in reality. It's hard, messy, and not easily captured by one benchmark. But if we get it right, the impact goes well beyond making nicer pictures.

The last change is more personal. I used to value being first. Now I value being right about direction, and being patient enough to work on something for years. The field moves so fast that it's tempting to chase every trend. But the work I'm proudest of came from staying with a question long enough to really understand it.

So in short: I moved from "is this new?" to "does this change what's possible, and for whom?"

r001.rationale: The response contrasts early emphasis on benchmark gains and being first with work that opens doors for others to build on and enables many future projects, presenting broader progress for the field as a measure of research value.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because my answer today is almost the opposite of what it was when I started.

When I was a PhD student, and honestly for years after, I measured value the way the community taught me to measure it. Does the paper get into the top conference? How many citations? Is the method novel? Novelty was the currency. You'd look for a gap in the literature, find a clever trick nobody had tried, show it beats the baseline by a point or two, and that felt like success. I published a lot of papers like that. I'm not ashamed of them, but if I'm honest, most of them didn't matter.

The shift happened when I started working on things that people actually used. At NVIDIA, with work like pix2pixHD and the image-to-image translation line, and later with the generative models, I started getting emails from people I'd never met. Artists. Game developers. People building products. And they weren't asking about the architecture. They were asking, "Can I run this on my machine? Why does it fail on this input?" That changed something for me. I realized the value of research isn't in the paper, it's in what happens after the paper. Does it unlock something that wasn't possible before? Does it become a building block that other people stack on top of?

So now I think about it in terms of a few questions. First, is this a problem where, if we solve it, the world is meaningfully different? Not the leaderboard, the world. Second, is the solution simple enough and robust enough that it survives contact with reality? A lot of beautiful ideas die the moment you give them real data. And third, does it compound? The best research I've been part of wasn't the cleverest. It was the stuff that became infrastructure, that other teams picked up without even citing us because it had become obvious.

That last one was hard to accept, by the way. Your ego wants credit. But the highest compliment in research is when your idea becomes so standard that people forget it was ever an idea.

I'd also say I've become much more skeptical of incremental work dressed up as breakthroughs, including my own. When I review now, I ask myself, if this paper disappeared tomorrow, would anyone notice in two years? Usually the answer is no. And that's okay, not everything has to be foundational. But we should be honest about which kind of work we're doing.

The other big change is about timing and scale. Earlier I thought a good idea was enough. Now I believe the idea is maybe a third of it. The rest is the data, the compute, the engineering discipline, and the patience to keep pushing when the first ten versions don't work. Generative models, world models, these are not a weekend of inspiration. They're years of grinding. Research that's valuable today often looks a lot more like building than like discovering, and I've made peace with that. Actually, I've come to enjoy it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts leaderboard performance and beating baselines with research that becomes infrastructure or a building block others can use, framing that contribution as a better measure of value.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become less focused on whether an idea looks impressive on its own, and more focused on whether it helps us make progress on a meaningful problem. An elegant method is valuable, but you also have to ask: What does it enable? Can other people build on it? Does it change what we’re able to do?

At the same time, I wouldn’t equate value with immediate usefulness. Some research is valuable because it opens a question that we didn’t know how to ask before. So, for me, it’s a balance: having a clear reason to care about the problem, while leaving room for ideas whose impact we can’t fully predict.

r001.rationale: The response values making progress on meaningful problems and enabling others to build on research, but it does not identify improving the research field as an alternative to outperforming other researchers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become less focused on whether a particular result looks impressive and more focused on whether it changes what we can do or how we understand a problem. A benchmark improvement can be useful, but the deeper question is: What did we learn? Does that insight help someone take the next step?

There’s also a balance between having a practical impact and exploring something whose value isn’t obvious yet. You don’t want every research project to be driven by an immediate application. Sometimes the most valuable contribution is finding a new way to frame a question. So I would say my view has broadened: research can be valuable because it solves a problem, but also because it opens up a direction that other people can build on.

r001.rationale: The response values changing what researchers can do or understand and opening directions for others, but it does not identify improving the research field as an alternative to outperforming other researchers.
